title: Chitrakoot
hook: you can still walk barefoot around the hill where the exiles lived
carry: reading the story with your feet

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot, the bright mountain, and your line, a parnashala, a house of leaves. Valmiki welcomed the exiles into his own story.

Most stories happen in places you can't go. Nobody can buy a ticket to Middle-earth. But on the border of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh there's a small town called Chitrakoot, with a green hill, a river and a lot of temples. Every day pilgrims arrive, take off their shoes, and start walking around the hill where, they believe, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana once lived in a hut of leaves.
screen: `PLACES YOU CAN'T GO.` → `A TOWN CALLED CHITRAKOOT.` → `PILGRIMS TAKE OFF THEIR SHOES.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Chitra means bright, wonderful, many-colored; kuta means a peak. The bright peak. In Hindi it's usually said Chitrakoot. Valmiki names a river there, the Mandakini, and it still runs through the town. Its main bathing place is Ram Ghat, where in the evenings people float lamps on the water. The hill at the center is Kamadgiri, often explained as the hill that grants wishes. Pilgrims walk all the way around it, often barefoot, stopping at shrines on the path. Walking around something holy, keeping it on your right, is called parikrama, and Hindus honor temples, rivers and hills this way. There's another layer. Chitrakoot is linked with the poet Tulsidas, who retold the Ramayana in Hindi, and a well-known tradition says that at Ram Ghat he was granted a vision of Rama. So the town carries two Ramayanas at once, Valmiki's Sanskrit and Tulsidas's Hindi. For pilgrims, the Ramayana isn't only a book. Its places are real places, and walking them is reading the story with your feet. Scholars debate which modern sites match which verses, and the text doesn't settle every question. The pilgrims aren't waiting for them. Every morning, they take off their shoes and walk.
screen: `CHITRA AND KUTA: THE BRIGHT PEAK.` · `THE MANDAKINI AND RAM GHAT.` · `KAMADGIRI AND THE PARIKRAMA.` · `TULSIDAS'S VISION AT RAM GHAT.` · then, large: `READING THE STORY WITH YOUR FEET.`

segments.voice: If you can, slip your shoes off, the way pilgrims do at the foot of the hill, and feel the floor under your bare feet: cool or warm, hard, pressing back. Let your breath slow and keep your attention low, in the soles. Nowhere to get to; just this ground.
Chitrakoot, today. A pilgrim town on the Mandakini, where people walk barefoot around Kamadgiri hill and read the Ramayana with their feet.
Your line: reading the story with your feet. For pilgrims, the Ramayana has an address. See you tomorrow.
